newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Business leaders seek to spur APEC into action.
newsitem.headline: Business leaders seek to spur APEC into action.

text.p: Top business executives advising Asia-Pacific nations on setting up the world's biggest free trade zone are becoming impatient with the slow rate of progress and want political leaders to share their sense of urgency.
"We must move more aggressively than we have been doing," Roberto Romulo, chairman of the APEC Business Advisory Council, told reporters in Manila at the weekend.

Romulo, a former Philippine foreign minister, said the 50 top executives who serve on the council want to advance the current timetable for the removal of all trade barriers among the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation forum's 18 member economies.
APEC has agreed that developed economies should drop all trade barriers by 2010, and less well-off nations should follow suit by 2020.

The business advisors, however, want this brought forward to match that of a proposed Southeast Asian free trade area that has a timetable of 2003 for a zero-to-5.0 percent tariff structure, Romulo said.

The advisors, from a wide range of business sectors from finance to construction, are also impatient with the slowness with which APEC policies on cross-border investment flows and economic and technical cooperation are being put into effect.
Part of the impatience stems from the private sector chief executives, who are used to getting things done quickly, having to deal with government bureaucrats.
"We get things done or we'd get fired," said Romulo, who is chairman of Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co.

ABAC is due to present its first comprehensive list of recommendations on October 24 to Philippine President Fidel Ramos, chairman of this year's summit of APEC leaders that will be held on November 25 in Subic Bay north of Manila.
Romulo declined to give details of the report but said one of the main thrusts would be to give private business a leading role in liberalising trade in the region.
While governments would provide the broad legislative and policy framework, it would be up to the private sector to identify specific projects to work on.
The business executives are also proposing financial incentives including slightly cheaper private funding for projects that advance APEC's cause.
"The private sector is saying...listen to us and we will give you some carrots, and if you don't listen to us we will not be so forthcoming about coming into your economies," Romulo said.
Ramos has already said he wants to ensure that the private sector is given a more prominent role in driving APEC forward than has previously been the case.
An APEC Business Forum to be attended by some 400-500 corporate leaders will also be held in Manila in November.
The national leaders will be invited to attend a meeting and banquet with the private sector executives on the eve of their Subic summit.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore and the United States.
